# Backlog snapshot — `public.backlog_items`

This file is generated by `scripts/export-backlog-snapshot.js` from the Supabase table
`public.backlog_items` -- it is NOT hand-maintained and must not be edited directly. The
table IS the authoritative source of truth for backlog content as of SES-83 phase (d)
(v7.0.112, 2026-08-21, John's call): runner work selection reads it via SQL and no longer
parses the markdown backlog files under `docs/`, which are being trimmed to pointers over
the remaining phases. This snapshot is therefore the table's authoritative offline and
git-history copy, not a secondary mirror -- the backup gap SES-81
identified, where the table had no point-in-time recovery path independent of Supabase's own
backups. Every runner ship point regenerates this file and commits it if changed, so
`git log` on this path is a durable history of the table's state across sessions.

**Tickets:** 678 · **Payload sha256:** `8d91d17d5cb3b55e50a45bd1268146160a5331d4e1a14ea45541529abd0c657a`

Cell escaping (applied in this order so it is mechanically invertible): a literal backslash
`\` becomes `\\`, a literal pipe `|` becomes `\|`, and a literal newline becomes the
two-character sequence `\n`. Unescaping reverses this in a single left-to-right pass over
those same three sequences -- escaping backslash first guarantees no bare `\` can appear in
an escaped cell except as the first character of `\\`, `\|`, or `\n`, so the pass is
unambiguous. An EMPTY cell (zero characters) means the stored value is SQL `NULL`. A stored
value that is itself the empty string is written as the literal two-character marker `\e`
-- escaping can never produce `\e` on its own (every backslash it emits is followed only by
`\`, `|`, or `n`), so `\e` is unambiguous as the empty-string marker.

Every cell is padded with EXACTLY ONE space on each side, and a reader removes exactly one
character from each side rather than trimming -- four tickets store values with their own
leading or trailing whitespace, and a `.trim()` reader would silently eat precisely those.
`tier` and `source_file` come from each section heading; the other twelve fields come from the
row. `parseDocument()` in the generating script is the reference reader and restores this
file to the exact table contents.

The final `Epic` column (SES-110) is `epics.name` joined through `backlog_items.epic_id` --
the NAME, not the uuid, because `epics.name` is UNIQUE and a restore should not depend on a
surrogate key surviving. An empty cell means the ticket belongs to no epic. The column is
appended LAST on purpose: the mirror reader in `scripts/check-session-docs.js` addresses cells
by index, so any other position would silently re-point every one of them.

`Design status` and `Kickoff` (SES-112) are the last two columns, appended for that same
index reason. `Design status` is why the ticket is not being built -- `auto` (Claude designs
it solo), `needs-john` (a decision only John makes), `needs-desktop` (the build needs an
attended session -- `.claude/` paths and other gated files), or `designed` (a kickoff doc
exists and `Kickoff` names it). An EMPTY `Design status` cell means SQL NULL: not yet
triaged. That is a real, deliberate value -- it is never to be read or restored as `auto`.

`History residue` (SES-115) is the last column and the only DERIVED one: rows are never
deleted from `backlog_items`, so a `done`/`removed` row sitting on the board is HISTORY, not
drift -- but such a row should have lost its queue number, its pin and its claim when it
closed. This cell names whatever is still set (`queue=N`, `claimed`, `pin=N`), and is EMPTY
for every active row and every clean history row. A LIVE claim is deliberately not residue --
a cycle releases its claim only AFTER its push (John, `q-claim-release-order`), so this export
always runs while the shipping cycle still holds one; only an EXPIRED claim (24h) counts, which
is the case with a stranded ticket behind it. An empty column here is the healthy state;
a non-empty cell means a recompute was missed. It is derived rather than three raw columns
because `queue` and `claimed_at` are row churn -- exporting them would change this file on
nearly every run and destroy the byte-identical guarantee above.

| 46 | CHI-69 | Tech Debt | P9 - Bug Fixes | A crash in a direct Drawer child escapes the inline ErrorBoundary and takes down the page | open | S-future (design required) |  | **New, found 2026-07-23 during `S-CHI-66`'s own live QA — a limitation of the boundary that session had just shipped, not of the code it was protecting.** `CHI-66`'s inline boundary wraps `Drawer`'s children as `<ErrorBoundary variant="inline">{children}</ErrorBoundary>`, returning `this.props.children` directly from `render()`. **An invalid object placed as a *direct* child of a `Drawer` therefore escalates past that boundary and still takes the whole page down** to the root fallback. Verified live, twice, with stack traces distinguishing the two cases: a direct child throws via `throwOnInvalidObjectType → createChild → reconcileChildrenArray → finishClassComponent` — i.e. while reconciling the `ErrorBoundary` class component's *own* children, which React attributes to the boundary itself and so escalates upward — whereas the same object nested one level deeper (inside a `<p>`, which is exactly `CHI-65`'s real shape) throws via `updateHostComponent` on a fiber *below* the boundary and **is** caught. So the protection genuinely works for the crash it was built for; this is the one placement it structurally cannot cover. **Found only by accident** — the QA session's first probe happened to sit in that position. **Unverified fix hypothesis, do not build on it without testing:** having `render()` return `<>{this.props.children}</>` may push the children onto a Fragment fiber below the boundary and close the gap at zero DOM cost. A wrapper `<div>` would also work structurally but is **not** acceptable as-is — `Drawer`'s content div is `flexDirection:"column"` with `gap:10`, so an extra element would collapse the spacing between every drawer's children. Needs a session that actually tests both. Low likelihood in practice (nobody writes `{someObject}` deliberately) but `CHI-65` wasn't written deliberately either. |  |  |  |  |

Related, reusable, not a drop-in answer. Scope to decide in its own session: what durability actually means here (survive a crash? a refresh? a new tab? across days?), where it lives, and how it interacts with Clear (`CHI-04`) and Demo Reset. Larger than `CHI-66` was. |  |  |  |  |

That produces both false FAILs (a real `nowrap` further along the rule is never seen) and, worse, **vacuous PASSes** — the coding session planted a `#ff0000` mid-rule and the hex-literal check still reported clean. Fix is one line: blank all `${…}` to a placeholder before matching rule bodies. **Distinct from `SES-69`**, which is about a test re-declaring the thing it checks; this one reads the real source and is still wrong, about the source's own syntax. Any future kickoff asserting on `NET_CSS` inherits the bug. Post-beta. |  |  |  |  |

When a tie group straddles a 1,000-row page boundary, Postgres may order the tied rows differently between the two `.range()` calls, so a row can be skipped (or duplicated) — silently. Boundaries drift constantly because the platform logs continuously (~63 inserts observed in 20 minutes). **Pre-existing and screen-wide:** a skipped row is simply absent from Total Calls, Total Cost, By LLM, By Agent and By Service alike, so `LOG-97` adds no new exposure (its `costById.get(id) \|\| 0` degrades to omitting one row's pennies, never a wrong number). Fix is small and standard: add a unique secondary sort (`.order('id')`) so the page window is deterministic. Worth doing before anyone treats these totals as exact. **Second call site found 2026-07-29 (`S-LOG-112-design`, during live QA) and it is worse: `useAgentActivitySummary()`'s paged fetch (`useAgents.js` ~157-166) has NO `.order()` at all** — 17 `.range()` pages over ~16.4k rows with unspecified ordering, so rows can be skipped or duplicated between pages. Feeds the whole CHI Agents drawer (Calls, Avg Cost, byKind, pattern rows). | 151 | HAR-03 | Speed | P9 - Bug Fixes | Nothing threads a cancellation signal into execute.js, so a client-driven hop loop cannot be stopped | open | S-future (design required, harness-level) |  | **P9 - Bug Fixes.** **New, found 2026-07-16 during `S-CHI-04-design` while scoping the Clear/Agent-Routing fix.** `resolveInProgress()`/`callCapability()` (`MarketIntelligenceScreen.jsx`) run a client-driven continuation loop against `api/capabilities/execute.js` — each hop is its own `fetch()` POST, and the client decides whether to fire the next `{action:"continue", job_id}` call. Nothing today threads a cancellation signal into `execute.js` itself, so whichever single hop is actively running on the server at the instant a user hits Clear (or otherwise abandons a request) keeps running to completion server-side, burning its own bounded LLM cost even though the client has already discarded interest in the result. `CHI-04`'s frontend generation-counter guard stops the *client* from continuing the chain or displaying a stale result, but does not (and structurally cannot, without this) kill the one in-flight hop itself. Fix would need a real cancellation flag (e.g. checked at each hop boundary in `execute.js`, or an `AbortController`-driven dropped-connection signal — unconfirmed whether Vercel's runtime reliably kills execution on a dropped client connection, would need verification) — harness-level, touches the shared execution path every capability goes through, not MI-specific. Bounded cost (one wasted hop, not unbounded), not a live blocker — deliberately not folded into `CHI-04`. |  |  |  |  |

| 1 | SES-146 | Tooling | P10 - Tooling | The settings gate never sees a scheduled cycle — scheduler_gate() misreads the trigger line the runbook tells every cycle to pass | done | cycle 72561db3 |  | FOUND LIVE 2026-08-23T13:44Z by cycle 72561db3 while executing step 1b, not reasoned about. TWO independent defects in public.scheduler_gate() (SES-143, v7.0.182), both of which silently disable John's §2b Automation interval. Both fail OPEN, so nothing has broken and nothing in the ledger shows it.\n\nDEFECT 1 — THE CONTRACT MISMATCH. runner-cycle.md step 1b tells every cycle, verbatim, to pass "<your prompt's trigger: line, verbatim>", and the routine prompt's line reads "trigger: scheduled". The function tests v_scheduled := (coalesce(p_trigger,'') = 'scheduled') — exact equality against the bare word. So a cycle that follows the runbook LITERALLY (which the stored prompt commands: "execute it EXACTLY") passes "trigger: scheduled", never matches, and takes the fail-open branch "not a scheduled cycle — your scheduler setting governs scheduled fires only". Pacing is then skipped entirely. NEGATIVE CONTROL, run live on this cycle's own id: p_trigger='trigger: scheduled' -> reason "not a scheduled cycle"; p_trigger='scheduled' -> reason "manual fire (started off the cron grid)". Same cycle, same instant, two different classifications. The five paced rows to date (06:41Z, 07:41Z, 10:41Z and two earlier) all passed the BARE word, i.e. every cycle so far interpreted the instruction loosely and got lucky.\n\nDEFECT 2 — THE GRID TEST MEASURES THE WRONG CLOCK. v_manual := v_scheduled and v_dist > 2, where v_dist is the circular minute distance between p_started and runner_settings.cron_minute (40). Cycles pass now() at the moment they reach step 1b, NOT the moment the routine fired. This cycle fired at 13:40:52Z and reached the gate at 13:43:12Z — dist 3 — so even with the bare word it is classified "manual fire … never paced" and exempted. Any cycle whose step-0/0b work takes more than ~2 minutes is silently exempt from John's interval. Predecessors reached the gate inside 2 minutes and so were paced; this one did not, because step 2 now reads a 65k-token runbook.\n\nNET EFFECT: John's Automation panel interval is inert for any cycle that either follows the runbook literally or is slower than ~2 minutes to step 1b. scheduler_on=false is unaffected (that branch is reached only when v_scheduled is true, so it is inert on the same path — worth checking in the fix).\n\nFIX SHAPE (one migration + one runbook line): normalise the trigger inside the function — strip a leading "trigger:" and whitespace, lowercase, then match — so both forms work and the runbook's verbatim instruction becomes true; and take the grid test off now() by passing the fire time, or widen/remove the tolerance, deciding explicitly rather than by accident. THE MECHANISM, in three facts that only bite together: (1) the published page is 132KB and BOTH read paths truncate it — WebFetch returns a head that cuts off mid-`briefing-state`, and the Artifact read does the same; (2) the full copy each one saves lands under `~/.claude/.../tool-results/`, which `SES-96` forbids an unattended cycle from shell-processing (the permission gate only a human can see, register B39); so (3) a rebuilding cycle CANNOT obtain the complete `briefing-state` it is required to re-seed, and re-seeding an incomplete one silently deletes John's history — the exact failure `SES-132` shipped §9.1 to end, arriving by a different route. WHAT SAVED THIS CYCLE, and it is luck rather than design: `public.runner_card_asks` stores BOTH halves of every thread (`question` AND `answer`), so the 8 live threads were reconstructed exactly from the DB over PostgREST with nothing transcribed by hand. THE REAL GAP IS THE REMAINDER: a cycle's own FOLLOW-UP entries on a thread — the "[runner, <ts>] ..." pairs a rebuilding cycle appends to tell John what became of his line — are written into `briefing-state` ONLY. They have no table, so the next rebuild must carry them forward from a page it cannot fully read. Measured tonight: 6 such entries existed across 5 threads (the 01:20Z set plus this cycle's own), and every one had to be re-typed into the build script from context rather than read from a row. A cycle whose context does not happen to contain them drops them, and John sees his thread lose its most recent reply. THE FIX, one shape, not a new mechanism: give a runner follow-up the same home John's ask already has — either a `runner_card_asks` row with `target_kind='runner-followup'` (question = the runner's headline, answer = the body, `asked_at` = when it was written), or a sibling table keyed the same way — and make the rebuild derive `briefing-state.asks` ENTIRELY from the DB, ordered by timestamp, with nothing hand-carried. That also makes the rebuild independent of being able to read the published page at all, which is the property actually worth having. SECOND, SMALLER: the same argument applies to `briefing-state.unblocks` and to any future page-only key — the standing rule should be that NOTHING lives only in `briefing-state`, because `briefing-state` is the one store this platform cannot reliably read back. Filed by cycle 76fa8b54 (v7.0.171).\n\n— SECOND INDEPENDENT HIT, cycle cceb3016 (v7.0.178), 2026-08-23T04:1xZ. Confirms this ticket from a different direction and names the exact mechanism that stops a rebuild. (1) THE READ HALF reproduced: Artifact action=read on the briefing URL returns the FRAME RUNTIME preamble as its head, not the page body, and saves the real 162.8KB HTML to /root/.claude/projects/<proj>/tool-results/artifact-*.html. briefing-state was recoverable only by Grep + a single-line Read against that path — the Read TOOL, never Bash, because runner-cycle.md step 9 / SES-96 forbid any Bash command against a ~/.claude/ path. So the state IS readable, with effort. (2) THE HALF THAT ACTUALLY BLOCKS THE REBUILD, and it is not the read: briefing-template.html ships briefing-state EMPTY ({"items":{},"directive":"",...}), so a cycle rebuilding from the template must RE-EMIT John's entire accumulated state or wipe it. That state currently holds 8 ask targets carrying ~19 entries — 8 of them John's own typed words, the rest prior runners' replies — roughly 15KB of nested-escaped JSON prose. The only programmatic splice would need a Bash/node read of the saved file under ~/.claude/, which is exactly the forbidden path; the only compliant alternative is a cycle hand-transcribing John's recorded history from its own context. THIS CYCLE DECLINED TO DO THAT and published nothing, on the asymmetry: a stale page costs one cycle of delay on cards that are durably in runner_items (register B18 rebuilds them FROM the DB, so nothing is lost), while a silent transcription error inside John's own recorded words is unrecoverable and invisible — and SES-132 shipped specifically so those threads would persist. (3) THEREFORE THE FIX HAS A SHAPE: the blocker is not "the page is hard to read", it is "state carry-forward has no machine path a cycle is permitted to use." Candidates: a Supabase-side store of briefing-state so the template can be filled from the DB like every other section (removes the page as the sole home of that history, which is this ticket's own title); or an explicit sanctioned exception letting a cycle splice the saved artifact file programmatically. Cost of leaving it: every unattended cycle's cards reach John only when an attended session rebuilds the page. The cloud container's egress proxy DENIES `deepbench.roadmapventure.com`: `curl` gets 403 on CONNECT (logged by the proxy itself as `connect_rejected` in `__agentproxy/status` → `recentRelayFailures`), and `WebFetch` returns `EGRESS_BLOCKED`. `api.vercel.com` IS reachable (308), so this is a host-level policy, not general egress loss. CONSEQUENCE: runner-cycle.md step 4 (blocker sweep #1, "verify dev serves … a user-blocking failure preempts everything") and step 8 (sweep #2, "if your own ship broke dev, revert-forward immediately") CANNOT RUN in an unattended cycle. A cycle that ships a `src/`/`api/`/`lib/` change therefore has no way to detect that it broke the site, and the revert-forward path that depends on sweep #2 is unreachable. Cycles have been recording "not observed" rather than inventing a deploy-state claim (correct), but that means the platform's only automated user-blocking-failure detector is dark. FIX OPTIONS, John's call: (a) add the production host to the environment's network egress allowlist (cheapest, and the only one that restores the sweep as written); (b) probe through an already-allowed path — the Vercel API is reachable, so a deployment-state + last-build-status check is weaker than a real HTTP GET of the page but is not nothing; (c) accept the gap explicitly and downgrade both sweeps to "attended sessions only", which means an unattended cycle may never ship a user-visible change. NOT worked around by this cycle: `SES-128` touched no `src/`/`api/`/`lib/` file, so nothing it shipped could have broken dev. | Selfbuild M3 - Independent Verification |  |  |  |

| 82 | LOG-07 |  | P9 - Bug Fixes | Fire-and-forget logActivity() can drop log rows when the serverless function tears down | open | S-future (design required — real ~33% drop rate now measured on `api/brief.js`, worth prioritizing above other `S-future` items; investigate await-with-bounded-timeout vs. current fire-and-forget) |  | **Found 2026-07-16 during `AA-192a`'s own live QA (one supplementary call dropped); confirmed with a real measured rate during `AA-192b`'s close-out the same day.** `logActivity()` (`lib/activity-log.js`) fires an un-awaited `fetch()` to Supabase and returns immediately; if the calling route also doesn't await it (true of every current caller — fire-and-forget is the documented design), a serverless function can return/tear down before the outbound write completes, silently dropping the log row with no error surfaced anywhere. **`AA-192b`'s design session directly measured this against the real deployed `api/brief.js` endpoint (3 real HTTP calls, not an in-process test): 2 of 3 produced a real `ai_activity_log` row, 1 never did (confirmed missing several minutes later, ruling out simple replication lag).** Also caught the same session: a coding session's own "live QA" cited a stale pre-existing row (from `AA-192a`'s earlier test) as if it were fresh evidence from its own call — a real process gap (accepting a report without independently confirming the row's timestamp is genuinely new), not just the underlying drop bug. This is a platform-wide reliability gap in the shared function itself, not specific to any one session's files — affects every one of the ~10+ existing `logActivity()` call sites (`AA-190`'s full migration, `AI-55`, `AI-56`, `AA-192a`/`b`, etc.), all sharing this same fire-and-forget shape. Non-streaming routes (like `api/brief.js`) that log immediately before returning likely have less real wall-clock grace time for the write to complete than streaming routes (like `api/plan.js`) that keep the connection open longer — a plausible reason this hadn't been directly measured before. |  |  |  |  |

| 109 | AA-111 |  | P2 - Inventive | Ephemeral/dynamically-synthesized Competency — raised in conversation (2026-07-04, John), not yet designed. | open | S-future (design required) |  | **Ephemeral/dynamically-synthesized Competency — raised in conversation (2026-07-04, John), not yet designed.** Idea: instead of only assembling a pre-existing, persona'd Agent's Skill Profiles at call time, an orchestrating agent (or the harness) could assemble a *novel* combination of Skill Profiles at runtime — a bespoke, one-shot worker with no name/avatar/Bench seat — run it once, and let it not persist afterward. Maps onto an already-legitimate but unused concept in `ARCHITECTURE.md` §2's own model: a "Standalone Competency" (a Competency with no persona is already valid/sellable/MCP-accessible) — the novel part is *runtime, ad hoc assembly* of one rather than a pre-built standalone Competency. Open questions before this can be scoped: (1) does "ephemeral" mean selecting/recombining *existing* Skill Profile rows at runtime (small, compatible extension of `assemblePrompt()`), or *synthesizing brand-new* Skill Profile content on the fly (much bigger claim — who reviews/approves it before it's trusted with real data access?); (2) governance must travel with it regardless of persistence — same `data_room_tag`/`uber_access` checks, same `ai_activity_log` attribution, same `reasoning`-field discipline as any other Agent Loop decision — "doesn't persist" must never mean "doesn't get logged or access-checked"; (3) the decision to synthesize a new configuration instead of reusing an existing agent is itself consequential and should pass `§19d`'s sniff test, not bypass it. |  |  |  |  |

Fix direction: give `plan.js`'s `prompt-service` action the same hybrid budget-check/checkpoint pattern `execute.js`'s `runLoop()` already proves out, or move Work Order creation onto `execute.js`'s generic capability path entirely rather than maintaining a second bespoke pipeline. Filed to the GENERAL board deliberately, NOT to a Selfbuild epic (closure discipline).\n\nSUBSTANCE. An authenticated /admin briefing screen inside the deepbench app replaces the artifact-as-buffer design end to end. John's taps POST to an API route holding server-side credentials and validating input; that route writes public.briefing_comments and the runner_ tables directly. The screen renders live from the DB. The rebuild -> republish -> read-back -> harvest machinery is then RETIRED ENTIRELY: no page to republish, no HTML to parse, no size budget to sink under, and no window in which a cycle can publish over un-harvested taps.\n\nWHY IT IS WORTH FILING NOW rather than when the project ends: every defect in the SES-188 family is a property of reading John's decisions back out of a document's own bytes. v7.0.223 trimmed 42,025 chars of comments to buy head room and said on its own stamp that it only moved the ceiling; v7.0.232 (this cycle) pinned the state block above every growth surface we control. Both are real fixes to the offset and neither touches the mechanism. This ticket is the mechanism.\n\nPREREQUISITE QUESTION #1 — JOHN'S AUTH STORY, and it is the reason this cannot be designed unattended. An IP gate is insufficient: a household shares an IP, so an IP allow-list authenticates the building, not the person. Clerk is the standing candidate (see ADM-1, the Super Admin screen this would live behind), but which identity story the app adopts is John's architectural call and it gates the whole design.\n\nEVIDENCE POINTERS (2026-08-24): gated card 18b8fdd8 — the card that put candidate 2 back to John and established that "the page writes directly to Supabase" has exactly one implementation, the artifact mcp capability, i.e. his own connector inside the page; John rejected it outright ("no credentials or connector channel in the page, ever").
